The Third Variable Problem (population size affects both)

The participants' anxiety scores at the end of the month
Whether participants used the mindfulness app
The number of participants in each group

Before beginning a new study on memory, a team of researchers must first submit their research proposal to a university committee that reviews it to ensure the study is ethical and protects participants' rights and safety. This committee is called the:

An evolutionary psychologist explains that humans commonly crave high-calorie, high-energy foods because ancestors who sought out these calorie-dense foods were more likely to survive periods of famine and pass down their genes. This principle, first proposed by Charles Darwin, is called:
Twin A and Twin B formed when a single fertilized egg split into two separate embryos, giving them nearly identical genetic material. What type of twins are Twin A and Twin B?
A pianist consciously decides to move her fingers across the keys to play a specific song. Which division of the nervous system directly carries this voluntary command to her skeletal muscles?

A person is fully relaxed on the couch, breathing slowly, with a low resting heart rate, and easily digesting a recent meal. Which system is primarily active during this state?
When a neuron receives a signal, it uses this branch-like structure to receive incoming messages from other neurons. This structure is called the:

Neurons follow the All-or-Nothing Principle, firing at full strength every time or not at all
Neurons only fire when a person is consciously paying attention to a stimulus
Louder sounds always fail to reach the neuron's firing threshold

Naloxone (Narcan) binds to opioid receptor sites without activating them, physically blocking opioid molecules from docking there and immediately reversing an overdose. Naloxone is best classified as an:

A college student regularly drinks alcohol, which slows down her central nervous system activity, impairs her coordination, and reduces her reaction time. Alcohol is best classified as a:

A man is bitten by a dog as a child and, from then on, experiences intense, automatic fear whenever he sees any dog, even friendly ones. Which limbic structure is most heavily linked to this raw fear response?

A structure sitting on top of the brainstem receives incoming information from all the senses except smell and routes that data to the appropriate higher brain regions for further processing. This structure is the:

A patient can understand language perfectly and knows exactly what she wants to say, but after a stroke, she physically cannot produce coherent speech. Damage to which brain area, located in the left frontal lobe, best explains this deficit?

A person who has been blind since birth shows unusually strong touch and hearing abilities. Brain scans reveal that her occipital lobe, normally dedicated to vision, has been recruited to help process this touch and sound information instead. This reorganization is best explained by:
While drifting off to sleep, a man suddenly experiences a vivid sensation of falling and his body jerks, snapping him back awake. This experience is best described as a:

An EEG recording of a sleeping participant shows brief bursts of rapid brain activity believed to play a role in memory consolidation and protecting sleep from outside disturbances. This pattern indicates the participant is in:

During a specific stage of sleep, a sleeper's EEG shows fast, active brain waves nearly identical to being awake, yet his skeletal muscles are completely paralyzed and unable to move. This seemingly contradictory combination is why this stage is often called:

A psychologist explains that dreams are not hidden messages from the unconscious mind, but are instead simply the brain's attempt to make sense of random neural signals fired by the brainstem during REM sleep. This explanation reflects the:

A man's wife reports that he repeatedly stops breathing for several seconds throughout the night, followed by a gasping momentary awakening, leaving him exhausted despite spending eight hours in bed. Which disorder is most consistent with this description?
A young girl suddenly sits up screaming in intense fear during the deepest stage of her NREM sleep, but the next morning she has no memory of the episode at all. This is best classified as a:
With her eyes completely closed, a dancer can still accurately sense the exact position and movement of her arms, legs, and fingers as she performs a routine. This ability relies primarily on her:

Years of exposure to loud concerts permanently damages the delicate hair cells inside a musician's cochlea, resulting in significant, irreversible hearing loss even though his eardrum and middle ear bones are completely intact. This type of hearing loss is called:

A sound engineer determines that a very high-pitched tone stimulates a highly specific location toward the beginning of the cochlea's membrane. Which theory of pitch perception best explains how this high pitch is being detected?

After stubbing her toe, a woman instinctively rubs the area and reports that doing so genuinely makes the pain feel less intense. Which theory of pain best explains why rubbing an injury can reduce the perceived pain?

Unlike every other sense, which travels through the thalamus before reaching higher brain regions, this particular sense bypasses the thalamus entirely and goes directly to the olfactory bulb, which connects closely to the limbic system, explaining why it triggers such vivid emotional memories. This sense is:

A person holding a 5-pound bag can easily notice when 1 pound is added, but a person holding a 100-pound bag cannot notice that same 1-pound addition. This phenomenon, where a constant percentage rather than a constant amount is needed to notice a difference, is called:

A photographer walks from a bright, sunlit sidewalk into a dark movie theater and needs several minutes before he can see the seats around him clearly. Which retinal receptor is primarily responsible for this dark adaptation process?

A graphic designer can distinguish extremely fine details and vibrant colors while working under bright studio lighting, thanks to receptors concentrated near the center of her retina. Which receptor is she primarily relying on?

After staring at a bright green square for 30 seconds and then looking at a blank white wall, a viewer sees a reddish afterimage in the same shape. Which theory of color vision best explains this specific afterimage effect?

Standing in the pitch-black hallway of a house she has never visited before, a woman must feel the texture of the wall and the edge of a doorframe, slowly piecing these raw sensory clues together to figure out the layout of the space. This is an example of:

Right before walking down a hallway, a woman is told by a friend that the space is haunted. As she walks, she interprets every small creak in the floorboards and every shifting shadow as evidence of something sinister. This mental predisposition to interpret a stimulus in a certain way is called:

At a loud, crowded party, a woman is able to completely tune out the music and dozens of overlapping conversations to focus entirely on what her friend directly in front of her is saying. This ability is known as:

In the famous invisible gorilla study, participants who were asked to carefully count the number of basketball passes in a video frequently failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walk directly through the middle of the scene. This failure to notice an unexpected object because attention was focused elsewhere is called:

During a free kick, a spectator's brain automatically perceives the defenders as a single unified wall because they are standing shoulder-to-shoulder, tightly packed together in the same physical space. This Gestalt principle is called:

As a baseball flies closer and closer to a catcher's face, his eyes physically turn inward to keep tracking it, and his brain uses the resulting muscle strain to help judge exactly how close the ball is. This binocular depth cue is called:

In a photograph of a gravel road, the individual pebbles near the bottom of the frame look sharp, distinct, and highly detailed, while the same pebbles farther up the road blur together into a smooth, indistinct surface. This monocular depth cue is called:
When asked to picture a dog, most people immediately imagine an animal like a Labrador rather than a rare, unusual breed. The Labrador represents the:

A toddler who has only ever seen dogs points at a cow and confidently says Doggie! because it also has four legs and a tail. After his parents explain that cows moo instead of bark, he creates an entirely new mental category just for cows. This adjustment is called:

Instead of trying every possible number on his lock, a man decides to first guess his own birthday, reasoning that it's a quick, likely guess even though it isn't guaranteed to be correct. This fast, efficient rule of thumb strategy is called a:

Meeting a new coworker who is quiet, wears glasses, and enjoys reading during breaks, a man immediately assumes she must work in the IT department rather than in sales, simply because she matches his mental image of a typical IT employee. This judgment is best explained by the:

Despite finding a movie boring and poorly made within the first 20 minutes, a couple decides to sit through the entire painful two-hour film, reasoning that they already paid $15 each for their tickets and don't want that money to go to waste. This decision reflects the:

During a brainstorming session, a team is asked to generate as many different possible uses for an ordinary brick as they can think of, with no single right answer being sought. This kind of open-ended thinking is called:

Needing to prop open a heavy door but lacking an official doorstop, a man struggles for several minutes without realizing that the thick hardcover book sitting right next to him on the shelf would work perfectly. His inability to see this book as anything other than something to read is an example of:

Despite not consciously paying attention, he is able to accurately repeat his friend's last sentence word for word because the sound briefly lingered in his memory. This type of sensory memory is called:
To remember a new phone number just long enough to dial it, a man repeats the digits to himself over and over in his head. Which component of working memory is he relying on?

A student effortlessly remembers exactly what she ate for breakfast that morning and the specific route she walked to get to school, despite never having deliberately tried to memorize either detail. This is best described as:

While studying for her AP Psychology exam, a student has to deliberately focus, pay close attention, and consciously work to memorize dense vocabulary terms. This type of deliberate, conscious encoding is called:

Rather than simply memorizing a vocabulary word's spelling or sound, a student connects the word's actual meaning to a personal memory from her own life, creating an unusually strong and durable memory for that term. This deep encoding strategy is called:

A woman can vividly and consciously recall the specific details of her 10th birthday party, including who attended and what cake was served, and can easily describe this event to others. This type of memory is called:

Before going to bed, a man makes a mental note to remember to take his vitamins the following morning. This type of memory, focused on remembering to perform a future action rather than recalling the past, is called:

Instead of trying to memorize a 10-digit phone number as ten separate, isolated digits, a woman groups them into three smaller units, like 555-867-5309, making the number far easier to remember. This strategy is called:

To memorize the colors of the rainbow in order, a student uses the acronym ROY G. BIV, where each letter represents the first letter of a color. This memory aid, which organizes information in a quirky and memorable way, is called a:

Instead of cramming the night before her exam, a student studies her vocabulary flashcards for just 20 minutes every single day over the course of two weeks leading up to the test. This strategy of spreading out study sessions over time is called:

A researcher finds that students who studied vocabulary in short sessions spread out over two weeks scored significantly higher on a final exam than students who crammed the same total number of study hours into one night. A friend recites a 15-item grocery list out loud, and a woman later realizes she has almost completely forgotten items 6 through 10, the ones recited in the middle of the list. According to the Serial Position Effect, why did she likely forget these specific items?

The middle items were spoken in a much quieter, harder-to-hear tone of voice

Rather than simply repeating a new AP Psychology vocabulary word over and over, a student thinks about what the term actually means and connects it to a specific personal experience from her own life. This deeper strategy, which builds strong neural connections for long-term storage, is called:

This inability to recall very early childhood events is called:

After a severe head injury, a man can no longer recall his own childhood, his wedding day, or even his own name, yet doctors confirm he is still fully capable of learning and remembering new information from this point forward. This specific inability to recall memories from before the injury is called:

A woman in the early stages of a progressive, fatal neurological disease struggles to remember what she had for breakfast that same morning, yet she can still vividly recall detailed memories from her childhood many decades ago. Her disease typically attacks recent memories before older, more deeply consolidated ones. This disease is:

Taking a fill-in-the-blank test with no word bank provided, a student must generate each vocabulary term entirely from her own memory, without any answer choices to jog her recognition. This type of retrieval is called:

A student takes a multiple-choice exam and finds that seeing the four possible answer choices printed on the page makes it much easier to identify the correct one than if she had to write the answer from memory alone. This easier retrieval process is called:

A researcher famous for studying memory found that people lose a massive amount of newly learned information very quickly right after learning it, unless they actively rehearse it, but the rate of forgetting then levels off significantly over time. This famous finding is best known as the:
After recently changing his computer password, a man keeps accidentally typing his old, familiar password out of habit, even though he consciously knows it no longer works. This is best explained by:

This phenomenon, exposed by psychologist Elizabeth Loftus, is called:

A student takes the SAT, a test specifically designed not to measure what she has already learned, but instead to predict her future capacity and potential ability to succeed and learn new material in college. This type of test is called an:

Evaluating whether a test accurately captures the right underlying concept is called checking its:

This observed global rise in IQ scores over time is called the:

Before taking a challenging exam, a student is reminded that people from his particular demographic group are stereotypically known for excelling on this type of test, and this awareness alone actually boosts his confidence and improves his performance. This phenomenon is called:

After failing his first calculus test, a student says, I'm just naturally bad at math, and no amount of studying is ever going to change that, so there's no point in trying harder. This belief that intelligence and ability are fixed, static traits is called a:

Researchers debate whether a person's outgoing personality is primarily the result of an inherited genetic temperament or the result of being raised in a warm, socially encouraging household. This classic developmental debate is called:

One theorist argues that a child's vocabulary grows smoothly and gradually, adding a few new words every single day in tiny incremental steps. Another theorist argues that language ability instead develops in sudden, distinct leaps, remaining flat for a while before abruptly jumping to a whole new level of ability. This expensive and lengthy research method is called a:

Regardless of their culture or country of origin, virtually all human infants crawl before they walk, and no amount of practice or special training can make a baby walk months earlier than their body is biologically ready for. This natural, predictable, biologically driven process of development is called:

A pregnant woman is warned by her doctor that consuming alcohol during pregnancy can cross the placental barrier and cause severe, permanent birth defects and cognitive impairments in her developing baby. Alcohol, in this context, is best classified as a:

The moment a nurse gently strokes a newborn's cheek, the baby automatically turns her head toward the touch and opens her mouth, searching for a food source, without ever having been taught this behavior. This inborn, automatic survival response is called the:

Children who are exposed to a second language before the age of seven tend to become fluent with a native-like accent far more easily than adults who begin learning that same language later in life, though adults can still learn it with significantly more effort. This optimal but flexible window for language acquisition is called a:
During puberty, a teenage boy's testes fully mature and become capable of producing sperm, directly enabling his biological ability to reproduce. This physical change is best classified as a:

A toddler who has an existing mental framework for dog sees a horse for the very first time and, without changing his understanding at all, confidently calls it a big dog. This process of fitting new information into an existing mental framework is called:

While a child is learning to read, her older brother, who reads at a much higher level, patiently helps her sound out difficult words and understand the story. According to Vygotsky, the older brother is functioning as a:

A child cannot yet ride a bike completely alone, but she can successfully ride it with her father holding onto the back of the seat for support and balance. According to Vygotsky, this sweet spot between what she can do independently and what she can only achieve with guidance is called the:

Which type of intelligence remains stable or even increases throughout late adulthood?

The prefix un- doesn't form a complete word on its own, but it carries clear, standalone meaning, transforming happy into unhappy by adding the concept of not. This smallest unit of meaning within a language is called a:

A 3-month-old baby lying in her crib makes soft, repetitive, vowel-like sounds such as oo and ahh simply out of comfort and satisfaction, with no actual consonant sounds involved yet. This earliest vocal milestone in language development is called:

A 7-month-old baby is now rapidly repeating consonant-vowel combinations like da-da-da and ba-ba-ba over and over, practicing the physical mechanics of speech using sounds pulled from languages spoken all around the world, not just her own household's language yet. This stage of language development is called:

At around 24 months old, a toddler demands want cookie and later states daddy go, stripping away all non-essential filler words like articles and prepositions in favor of an abbreviated, highly efficient statement. This stage of language development is called:

A young child confidently declares, I goed to the park yesterday and saw three mouses, incorrectly applying the standard past-tense -ed rule and the standard plural rule to two irregular words that don't actually follow those patterns. This language learning error is called:

A child's father experiences a stressful, demanding schedule after his company implements a strict new overtime policy, and this added stress indirectly makes him more irritable and less patient with his son at home, even though the son has never even visited his father's workplace. This indirect environmental influence is called the:

During the Strange Situation procedure, a toddler clings desperately to her mother, becomes intensely distressed when separated, but then pushes her mother away angrily upon reunion while still clearly desperate for closeness, showing an unpredictable mix of neediness and resistance. This specific insecure attachment style is called:

A set of parents maintains high expectations for their children's behavior and achievement, but they also explain their reasoning behind household rules, listen to their children's opinions, and offer plenty of warmth and emotional support. This parenting style, which encourages independence and personal responsibility, is called:

A 16-year-old girl believes that no one, not even her own parents, could possibly understand the intensity and uniqueness of her personal heartbreak after a breakup, convinced that her emotional experience is entirely unlike anything anyone else has ever felt. This cognitive distortion, common during adolescence, is called the:

According to Erikson, a young child who is encouraged to plan and lead her own games during playtime develops confidence and leadership skills, while a child who is heavily restricted from taking any charge may develop a sense of inadequacy. This stage is called:

A 30-year-old woman feels significant social pressure and personal anxiety because she has not yet gotten married or had children, since her culture holds a shared, unspoken expectation that these milestones should typically happen by a certain age. This culturally shared timetable for major life milestones is called the:

In Pavlov's classic experiment, the food placed in front of the dog naturally and automatically triggers salivation without any prior learning being necessary at all. The food itself is best classified as the:

In Pavlov's classic experiment, a bell begins as a completely neutral sound that means nothing to the dog, but after being repeatedly rung right before food is presented, the bell alone eventually begins to trigger salivation. The bell, once it has taken on this new power, is best classified as the:

In this scenario, the anxiety triggered by the sound of the drill alone is the:

Why is this specific timing and order absolutely critical for successful conditioning?
The neutral stimulus must come before the unconditioned stimulus so the brain learns to anticipate the impending event
The order of presentation has no actual effect on whether conditioning will successfully occur
The unconditioned stimulus must always be presented before the neutral stimulus for any learning to happen

This sudden reappearance of the extinguished response is called:

After being bitten by a large black dog, a young boy becomes fearful and bursts into tears at the sight of any dog he encounters afterward, regardless of its size, breed, or color. This tendency to respond with the conditioned fear response to stimuli that are merely similar to the original one is called:

Unlike typical classical conditioning, which usually requires many repeated pairings to form a lasting association, taste aversion can form a permanent connection after just a single pairing of a food with subsequent illness. This unique, rapid form of associative learning is called:

A man quickly buckles his seatbelt every time he gets in his car specifically because doing so makes the annoying, repetitive beeping alarm stop immediately. Removing this unpleasant beeping sound to increase his seatbelt-buckling behavior is an example of:

After a teenager breaks his 10 PM curfew, his parents take away his phone privileges for an entire week, and as a result, he becomes much more careful about coming home on time going forward. Removing this desirable phone privilege to decrease his curfew-breaking behavior is an example of:

A trainer working with a dolphin cannot simply wait for it to accidentally perform a complete, complex jump-and-spin trick on its own. Instead, she first rewards the dolphin for approaching the hoop, then for touching it, then for swimming through it, gradually building up to the full trick over many sessions. This process of rewarding successive approximations toward a final goal behavior is called:

A child who is consistently praised by her parents for saying thank you at home begins to spontaneously say thank you to her teachers and classmates at school as well, even though she was never specifically rewarded for saying it in that new setting. This tendency to perform a reinforced behavior in new, similar situations is called:

A gambler keeps pulling the lever on a slot machine because she never knows exactly how many pulls it will take before she wins again, sometimes winning after just 3 pulls and other times after 50 pulls. This unpredictable reinforcement schedule, which produces the highest and most consistent rates of behavior and is incredibly resistant to extinction, is called:

A teenager checks his phone repeatedly throughout the day at a slow, steady, and fairly consistent rate, since he never knows exactly when a friend might text him back and the wait time varies unpredictably each time.
